analysis.one_liner: Lets workers opt out of forced arbitration in their employment contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or any cosponsors in the 109th Congress, ending when that Congress adjourned in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal arbitration law so that an employer could not force an employee to sign away the right to go to court as a condition of getting or keeping a job. Arbitration of a workplace dispute would be used only if, after the dispute arises, one side requests it in writing and the other side agrees in writing within 60 days. It applied to contracts created or renewed after enactment. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, especially those at companies that require signing arbitration agreements as a condition of employment. They would keep the option of taking discrimination, harassment, wage, and other employment disputes to court instead of being locked into a private arbitration process chosen by their employer, where proceedings are confidential, discovery is limited, and there is no appeal.

how_it_helps.text: An employer could not require an employee to arbitrate a dispute as a condition of employment, so workers could not be hired or fired contingent on giving up their day in court.

Arbitration could be used only if, after a dispute actually arises, one party submits a written request and the other consents in writing within 60 days — replacing pre-dispute clauses signed at hiring with a genuine, case-by-case choice.
The bill applies to contracts entered into, amended, renewed, or extended after enactment, so it would cover new and rolling-over employment agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on mandatory arbitration clauses would lose their ability to route employee claims into a private, confidential process with no appeal, and would face more litigation in court. The private arbitration industry would lose a steady stream of cases that arrive through employers' pre-dispute clauses rather than a genuine choice.

drawbacks.text: Employers and arbitration proponents argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper for resolving disputes, and that moving claims into the courts would add litigation costs that could be passed on and delay resolutions for everyone involved.

By making arbitration available only by mutual written agreement after a dispute arises, the bill would eliminate arbitration even where an employee might prefer it — and would apply prospectively to all new and renewed contracts rather than only genuinely coercive ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gain is significant: a court offers public proceedings, fuller discovery, a judge, and a right of appeal, while mandatory arbitration puts the employer in the position of choosing the forum in advance and keeping the process private. The main cost falls on employers through increased litigation, and some workers who might have preferred quick arbitration lose that option too. The bill does not address all criticisms of arbitration (for example, consumer contracts), only employment, which limits its scope but also its disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill in the House on September 6, 2005, and it was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
On September 19, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, where it stayed.
The bill had no cosponsors and no further actions were taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with mandatory arbitration policies kept their current ability to require workers to sign away their day in court; the private arbitration industry kept the flow of cases created by pre-dispute employment clauses.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let employees accept or reject arbitration of employment disputes.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no recorded opposition but also no cosponsors, and never reached a vote, so no partisan division ever appeared on the record.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from requiring arbitration as a condition of employment and would require post-dispute written consent for arbitration, forcing more employment claims into court. Under the status quo outcome, they lost nothing.

industries.industry: Private arbitration providers (e.g., arbitration and mediation firms)
industries.note: Employers' pre-dispute clauses are the main channel supplying employment cases to arbitration firms; removing them would shrink that business. The bill entrenches nothing for them; it simply removes the pipeline.
